entries.title: Congressional Probe Finds Rep. Gooden May Have Misused Taxpayer Money
entries.summary: The Office of Congressional Conduct questioned luxury travel on his House account and campaign disbursements.
entries.content:
The Office of Congressional Conduct said Monday that Rep. Lance Gooden may have misused taxpayer money for luxury travel and “misreported or falsified campaign disbursements,” urging further review by the House Ethics Committee.

In a 36-page report released by the Ethics Committee, the OCC found that “there is substantial reason to believe that Rep. Gooden improperly sought travel-related reimbursement for non-official travel purposes,” and that Gooden and his campaign “may have knowingly misreported or falsified campaign disbursements” that had no legitimate political purpose.

The report takes issue with an alleged “pattern of extravagant expenditures” under his Members’ Representational Allowance, which is a taxpayer funded budget for lawmakers to pay for their official congressional duties — including travel and staff salaries.

The OCC initially referred the investigation to the House Ethics Committee on July 10, but the internal watchdog had not released its findings until Monday.

The four-term Texas Republican hit back in a statement shared with The Washington Sun, calling the OCC’s recommendation a “bogus referral” and a “witch hunt.”

The OCC questioned the purpose of Gooden’s stays at luxury hotels in addition to a duplicate airfare reimbursement that “seemingly covered his son’s travel costs.” The OCC also investigated alleged purchases and reimbursement of travel benefits booked though his wife’s account, a move barred by House rules.

“The frequency of brief stays at luxury hotels, often amounting to thousands of dollars per visit, raises legitimate questions as to whether such expenditures were reasonable under applicable House rules and standards,” the report says.

The OCC questioned extended car rentals as well as rideshares that appeared to be connected to campaign activity. Members of Congress can only use their federally funded budgets to pay for their official duties and are generally prohibited from using the funds to pay for campaign activities.

Gooden won reelection in Texas’ 5th Congressional District last week, besting Democrat Chelsey Hockett.

The OCC scrutinized 23 disbursements, amounting to $256,465.77, made to Chase Bank by Gooden’s campaign committee, Lance Gooden for Congress, from Jan. 1, 2025, to Feb. 11, 2026. The watchdog found discrepancies between “total credit card disbursements and the sum of their corresponding itemized entries,” by analyzing Federal Election Commission reports.

“At a minimum, these inconsistencies suggest deficient or negligent accounting practices,” the OCC wrote. “On the other hand, they raise concerns that the Campaign Committee may be misreporting financial activity to obscure potentially improper expenditures.”

In Gooden’s statement, he took aim at Omar Ashmawy, the chief counsel for the Office of Congressional Conduct, by highlighting a DUI charge he received in 2022 among other allegations.

"There’s a reason the Senate doesn’t have an OCC — because of insane, bogus referrals like this one,” Gooden said. “There is a rich irony in being investigated by disgraced OCC Director Omar Ashmawy, a man who can’t control his own conduct given his history of drunk driving and multiple abuse and assault allegations by women.”

Gooden also called for the House Administration Committee to launch an “oversight investigation into the OCC’s target selection and record of failed inquiries.”

Gooden and his “relevant staff” allegedly failed to comply with the OCC’s investigation, which means the watchdog was unable to discern whether or not the certain payments in question “were in fact a result of administrative oversight, or a more substantive irregularity.”

The congressman's attorneys refuted the OCC’s findings about Gooden’s lack of cooperation and described the OCC’s representation of its process as “fundamentally dishonest.”

“The OCC declined to narrow its request, declined to pose specific questions, and made no effort to engage with the practical burdens and privacy concerns imposed by a demand of this magnitude on an active Member of Congress,” the attorneys wrote in a July 16 letter addressed to House Ethics Committee chair, Rep. Michael Guest (R-Mississippi), and ranking member, Rep. Mark DeSaulnier (D-California).
entries.author: Jenna Monnin

entries.title: Haley Stevens Was in the Republican Cloakroom for Congress’ First Votes Back Since the Election
entries.summary: Reporters didn’t see the Michigan Democrat on the first day back in session since the midterms, but the House clerk recorded two “yea” votes from her.
entries.content:
Rep. Haley Stevens may be a pariah to her party, but she showed up to work on Monday night anyway, albeit practically in hiding.

A week after blowing up her professional life with her shocking endorsement of Michigan Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers, many wondered if Stevens would show her face in the Capitol again. Her colleagues have said she made a “terrible decision” and conducted a “despicable betrayal. They even said there is “not a place” for her in the Democratic caucus.

While she remained out of sight to reporters, it turns out Stevens spent Monday’s vote series in the Republican cloakroom just off of the House floor, multiple sources told The Washington Sun. The House clerk’s office shows she voted “yes” on two bills.

Stevens has kept a low profile since she was spotted going to vote on Election Day, accompanied by her mother and wearing a conspicuously large hat. Last week, she dropped out of the lineup for a post-election panel only to be roasted by Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Maryland), who filled in for her.

Several of her top staffers promptly quit after her last-minute endorsement of Rogers over now-Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed. While Stevens was back in town on Monday, whatever remains of her staff was apparently not.

Reporters for The Sun stopped by Stevens’ office three times on Monday — in the morning, at noon and around 6 p.m. — and found a locked door. Nobody answered to knocks.

A large wooden box labeled “FRAGILE,” with one side open, sat empty outside the door.

One staffer for a nearby office said they had seen the door ajar at some point in the morning.

El-Sayed, the progressive Democrat who defeated Stevens in the Senate primary and prevailed against Rogers last week, spent the day at new member orientation, met with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and was swarmed by reporters whenever he was spotted in the hallways.

Stevens’ office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
entries.author: Reese Gorman, Chase Pellegrini de Paur, Hunter Riggall

entries.title: Federal Prosecutors in Western Washington State Will Let Many ICE Detention Cases Go Unopposed
entries.summary: The U.S. attorney’s office says it can’t keep up with the surge in immigration detention challenges.
entries.content:
Federal prosecutors in western Washington state say they are stretched too thin to fight every immigrant seeking release from detention, meaning many detainees will get a court ruling without facing government opposition.

Charles Neil Floyd, the acting U.S. attorney for the Western District of Washington, said that his office will begin declining to appear in court to fight many detention challenges filed against U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, he wrote in a recent letter to Chief U.S. District Judge David Estudillo.

“The large volumes of petitions that are being filed, often copying from other petitions, has severely impacted the government’s ability to respond,” Floyd wrote in the Oct. 26 letter. “Thus, going forward, in order to conserve resources, there will be many habeas cases in which the [U.S. Attorney’s Office] will no longer assume responsibility for providing a defense.”

Driven by President Donald Trump’s aggressive deportation campaign, an influx of immigration arrests have flooded the courts with habeas corpus petitions as detainees seek to challenge ICE holds. The administration also regularly denies bond hearings to many immigrants, which has contributed to the surge.

Between January 2025 and Nov. 3, there were about 2,000 immigration habeas petitions filed in western Washington, a district that handles nearly all of the state’s detention challenges, according to ProPublica. Earlier this year, judges reported working after-hours and on weekends to handle the influx of emergency motions, The Seattle Times reported.

Taking on every case consumes substantial time, Floyd wrote, “even after the petitioner has been released or received a bond hearing.” He added that the workload has made it harder to handle other civil cases.

Under the new policy, Floyd said the courts can “assume” that his office will not be challenging detainees if a government lawyer does not appear within seven court days of a scheduling order.

That scenario played out Saturday, when government lawyers didn’t show up to oppose the detention petition of Baljit Singh, an asylum seeker from India.

Singh was detained in September after he and friends inadvertently reached an exit at the Canadian border while visiting a state park, according to a complaint filed in federal court.

U.S. District Judge Tiffany M. Cartwright ruled the case as “intentionally unopposed” and ordered Singh be released within 24 hours. Floyd’s letter was included as an exhibit in that case, making it public.

entries.title: The Washington Sun Metro: The New Kid on the Block
entries.content:
Good morning. This is The Washington Sun Metro Newsletter for Nov. 10, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

In today’s newsletter: D.C.’s newest council member, bird-watching at East Po and Rowdy Audi.

Capital Weather’s Daily Digit — 8/10. A cold start, but sunny skies and highs near 70 more than make up for it. Read the full forecast.





THE LATEST

Elected officials often stick around for way too long. D.C.’s newest council member won’t have that problem.

Jamal Holtz was sworn in as an interim at-large council member on Monday afternoon, taking the seat once occupied by Robert White before he was elected D.C. delegate to Congress. Holtz’s appointment by the D.C. Democratic Party followed a week of unexpected political drama, and the position is only temporary — should he want to finish off White’s term, he’d have to win over D.C. voters in a special election that has been scheduled for April 6.

But Holtz made one thing clear: He’s not long for the office.

The 28-year-old native Washingtonian — the “first Gen Z member of the council,” he touted — says he not only won’t run in the special election, but also plans to step aside once the D.C. Democratic Party has wrapped up a formal process to identify another interim council member who can serve until the special election.

That means Holtz could be a sitting D.C. lawmaker for as little as a few weeks, and at most a few months. An interim-interim council member, if you will. “I am here to serve during a period of transition,” he told a large crowd of well-wishers in the Wilson Building on Monday. “Whether you serve for one day or one decade, the seriousness of public service doesn’t change.”

This short of a tenure could well be a first for D.C. Past interim council members have served anywhere from three to six months. It also presages what will be an unsettled six months to come for White’s old seat: Holtz will be a placeholder ahead of the Democratic Party’s next appointee, who would then have to compete in the April special election should they want to stay in office.

Holtz’s planned brief stay on the council has already prompted questions. Does he get a staff? Chairman Phil Mendelson said that while someone serving only a few weeks might not, he also doesn’t want Holtz to go staffless — especially with three critical legislative sessions before the close of the year. Will he be ready for big votes? Holtz said that he’s brushing up, and that multiple people have sent him the music video for Schoolhouse Rock’s famous “How a Bill Becomes a Law.” “That one was in my head the entire weekend,” he joked.

Holtz conceded that the entire situation is “unusual,” but also spoke about being profoundly honored by the opportunity. “To represent the residents of the District will represent the honor of my lifetime,” he said.





DEEP DIVE

birderspotomacpark_003.jpg (4032x2688, AR: 1.50)
The birds and the tees: Much to the dismay of area bird lovers, the Trump administration’s planned redevelopment of East Potomac Golf Links would effectively take away the No. 1 birdwatching spot in and around the nation’s capital.

The Sun’s Justice Covert reports that bird-watchers have tracked 272 bird species at Hains Point — the southernmost tip of the island — which is more than at a dozen other locations across northern Virginia and southern Maryland, according to eBird, a global online database that lets users log bird locations.

But the Interior Department plans to expand the proposed golf course over Hains Point and relocate the recreational areas that bird-watchers enjoy to nearby sites such as West Potomac Park and the Tidal Basin.

While the legal battle over the proposal continues, bird-watchers worry the damage is already done, since the government has already removed hundreds of trees from the park.

Ahead of East Potomac Park’s scheduled closing for renovations by Sunday, local bird advocacy groups held morning walks around Hains Point every day during the last week of October. One of the walks’ leaders told The Sun that she couldn’t imagine what it would be like to lose access to the area.

“I can’t even put it in my head,” she said. “Like many, many others, we hope that does not happen. It’s almost like a bad dream, like it’s not really happening. It’s terrible. It’s awful.”





FROM THE DISTRICT

You can’t park there: The Secret Service arrested two people near the White House yesterday morning after a car crashed onto the sidewalk near Lafayette Square and a person jumped a security barrier, The Sun’s Kendall Staton reports.

Pumping the brakes: A bill to legalize Waymo and other self-driving cars in D.C. may be on the rocks with the D.C. Council. The Sun has learned that three key lawmakers on the transportation committee are opposed, which could prevent the bill from moving forward.

One of them, Ward 5 council member Zachary Parker, said in a social media post he supports the tech but wants to “take a few more months” to work with Mayor-elect Janeese Lewis George to address labor displacement and safety concerns. “We’ll have a stronger bill for it,” he wrote.

A hotly anticipated shipment of trash cans, namely the 96-gallon “supercans” most D.C. residents use for city trash collection, has finally landed after being on back order for months. The Department of Public Works received 1,200 cans yesterday and will get another 1,200 next month to meet customer demand, interim Director Chris Rodriguez said in a video shared with The Sun.

A statue lampooning President Donald Trump’s bone spurs — one of the reasons he received deferments during the Vietnam War — popped up on the National Mall days before Veterans Day, The Washington Post reports. It’s the latest installation mocking the president from self-described “anonymous art collective” Secret Handshake.





FROM VIRGINIA

Bah, humbug! One of Northern Virginia’s largest Christmas markets was canceled just days before it was due to open last weekend, WUSA9 reports. The venue, Dulles Town Center Expo, didn’t have the required permits. That’s left about 200 vendors waiting on refunds for booth fees and without revenue they were counting on headed into the holidays.

Dulles International Airport unveiled a new concourse yesterday, wrapping up a three-year construction project, WTOP reports. The 14 new gates, restaurants, expanded seating areas and new lounges will add needed capacity to an airport reporting record passenger growth. The first flight out of the newly minted Concourse E departs today.





WHAT YOU GET WITH WATER VIEWS

Maryland Real Estate (6000x4000, AR: 1.50)

This week’s real estate column looks at what buyers can get for under $1 million with water views in the D.C. area.

Where is this house listed? Click on your guess to see the answer:

A. Maryland

B. Virginia

C. D.C.





SPORTS

Home field advantage: The Spirit left no doubt in a dominant 4-1 win Sunday in the NWSL quarterfinals. But away from the field, there was plenty of uncertainty about what comes next. For a short period, a scheduling conflict was set to move Washington’s semifinal meeting with Utah from Audi Field to Northwest Stadium in Landover. But, as The Sun’s Emma Baccellieri details, team officials were able to find a last-minute solution. Crisis averted, Audi is expected to get rowdy on Saturday at noon.

The Commanders are running out of time. Not only is Washington clinging to the very edge of the playoff picture after a frustrating home loss to the Rams, but it now faces a short week with a critical game against the Giants on “Thursday Night Football.” The Sun’s Martenzie Johnson takes a look at the biggest problems with Sunday’s performance and whether coach Dan Quinn’s team can find solutions ahead of a must-win matchup.

What to Watch Today

NCAAM: Georgetown vs. Delaware State, 6:30 p.m. (ESPN+)

NHL: Capitals at Senators, 7 p.m. (Monumental)





Thank you for reading! If you liked this newsletter, please forward it to a friend. If someone shared it with you, please sign up — it’s free! Got a tip or comments to share? Email us at metro@washsun.com. Finally, the answer to yesterday’s trivia question was A) Banned horse-drawn carriages from public streets. That was the objective of a failed D.C. ballot initiative in 1991. A special shout-out to Rebecca Crumlish, who answered first.

The newsletter was produced by Jaden Amos, Michael Errigo and Nikie Johnson.

entries.title: Hegseth Vows to Keep Job While Impeachment ‘Circus’ Swirls
entries.summary: The defense secretary also claims that impeaching him is a step toward prosecuting troops.
entries.content:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth forcefully pushed back against a growing impeachment threat and questions about his leadership following Republicans' sweeping midterm losses, calling the articles of impeachment a “circus” and vowing to continue in the job.

“What one disgruntled and defeated congressman is attempting is not oversight, and it’s not accountability,” Hegseth said Tuesday at a Pentagon news conference, referring to new articles of impeachment filed against him. “It’s a farce, and it’s a stunt and everybody knows it.”

Hegseth’s remarks came a day after Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Kentucky) formally renewed his efforts to impeach the defense secretary, setting up a House vote on Tuesday. Massie accused Hegseth of violating federal law and the Constitution through his leadership of military operations and other actions at the Pentagon.

Massie, in a post on Tuesday, said the vote would likely be on a motion to refer the resolution to committee, which he said would kill it. “If we can overcome that effort, we will proceed to a real debate and vote on the Articles of Impeachment,” he said.

Hegseth’s defense also covered the Iran war, whose economic shock waves fueled Republican losses in last week’s midterm elections in which Democrats wrested control of both chambers of Congress.

Instead, Hegseth said that the Iran war will be viewed by history “differently than conventional wisdom right now.” President Donald Trump did the right thing for American security, he continued, not for politics.

Hegseth also claimed that the proceedings against him — which he called a “show trial” — are just a step toward putting American troops on trial for their actions under the secretary.

“If they want to come for the warriors, they’re going to have to come through me,” Hegseth said.

Asked if he called allies on Capitol Hill, Hegseth said there was “a ton of support” among congressional Republicans. “I am grateful that Republicans are taking a real look at this,” he said.

It was Hegseth’s first formal briefing since May, despite continued U.S. military operations against Iran and deadly strikes on suspected drug-trafficking vessels in Latin American waters.

Trump has defended Hegseth, citing the January operation that captured Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and U.S. attacks that he claims have devastated Iran’s naval and air forces.

But Iran has continued attacking American military installations across the Middle East and disrupting shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, sending oil prices higher during a war now in its ninth month. Trump declared Monday that the conflict was effectively over from a military standpoint and again suggested Tehran was eager to negotiate an agreement.

Trump, in a post Tuesday that was published minutes after Hegseth finished briefing reporters, said Hegseth gets an “‘A’ PLUS, PLUS, PLUS for his defense against” Massie, whom the president characterized as “disgruntled,” “angry” and “defeated.”

The first three articles focus on the War Powers Resolution, accusing Hegseth of participating in an unauthorized war against Iran, defying a congressional directive to end hostilities and continuing military operations beyond the law’s 60-day limit.

Other articles accuse Hegseth of dismantling safeguards intended to prevent civilian casualties, authorizing unlawful killings at sea and abusing his authority in seeking to punish Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Arizona).

Despite the push coming from a Republican lawmaker, Hegseth has repeatedly dismissed the impeachment effort as politically motivated and defended the military operations carried out under Trump.

Speaking to reporters on Monday, Hegseth called the efforts “noise” and said he would be happy to “litigate” the military actions “all day long.”

Hegseth also heaped praise on the new White House chief of staff, Stephen Miller. Without Miller in the administration, Hegseth said, international commitments to fighting drug cartels and a “secure southwest border” wouldn’t be possible.

“We've got no better friend at the Department of War than Stephen Miller,” Hegseth said. “He will fight and defend this republic, and we're proud to be right there with him all the way.”

The impeachment effort has gained support from House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries, who announced Sunday that he would vote for the resolution. Several Republicans have publicly questioned Hegseth’s leadership, but Massie has acknowledged that he has no commitments of support from his Republican colleagues.

The House is readying to take up impeachment as Republicans are still reeling from election losses blamed partly on the Iran war. But the outcome remains uncertain.

House Speaker Mike Johnson on Monday condemned the effort as a dangerous political stunt.

“Impeaching a Cabinet secretary right now, especially the Department of War in the middle of hostilities abroad, would be a terrible, terrible look, a terrible thing for our allies and our enemies to see that,” Johnson said.

Under House procedure, Johnson must take up Massie’s resolution within two legislative days of his formal notice. Opponents could move to table the measure or refer it to committee, which would effectively kill it.

Massie said Monday he expected House leaders to give Hegseth an opportunity to respond publicly before scheduling a vote.

“I would like to see him go through the eight articles of impeachment and just make the argument from a podium,” Massie said. “You can use notes. Get the lawyers to help you. Tell us why you are not guilty of each of these eight articles of impeachment. I hope that's what he does.”

Even if Hegseth survives the immediate challenge, he faces extensive congressional investigations when Democrats take control of the House and Senate in January.
entries.author: Joe Gould, Kyle Chouinard

entries.title: Federal Judge Dismisses a DOJ Lawsuit Challenging Montgomery County’s Gun Ban
entries.summary: The lawsuit argued the ban violated the Second Amendment.
entries.content:
A federal judge on Monday dismissed a Trump administration lawsuit that challenged a Montgomery County law banning guns within 100 yards of “places of public assembly,” such as schools and places of worship.

The Justice Department filed the lawsuit Aug. 3 in the U.S. District Court of Maryland, just a week after the law went into effect, arguing the local restrictions violated the Second Amendment right to bear arms. The DOJ brought the complaint under the authority of a 1994 law allowing the U.S. attorney general to sue local enforcement agencies for a “pattern or practice” that violates people's rights.

U.S. District Judge Theodore Chuang ruled that law did not give the administration the authority to challenge the local statute, writing that “the federal government should not have unfettered authority to intrude on the actions of state and local governments.”

Chuang, an Obama appointee, dismissed the lawsuit with prejudice, meaning it cannot be refiled. The Justice Department can appeal the decision.

Montgomery County Executive Marc Elrich said in a statement that the ruling affirms the county government’s responsibility and authority to safeguard its community. He said the county’s actions were grounded in the law and met the obligation of protecting the public.

“We should not have to choose between respecting constitutional rights and pursuing thoughtful, lawful measures to prevent gun violence,” he said.

The law still faces legal challenges. Rabbi Menashe Shapiro of the Silver Spring Jewish Center filed a separate lawsuit in July, alleging the statute violates his rights to religious freedom and makes it harder for Jewish synagogues to protect their congregations.

“This ban could not come at a worse time for Montgomery County’s Jewish community,” the complaint said, listing several prominent examples of violence against Jewish people. “Montgomery County seeks to deprive Jews of their ability to defend themselves at their most Jewish moment: praying in synagogues. Jewish law requires Jews to defend themselves when necessary. Montgomery County would rather declare open season.”

Legal proceedings in the Silver Spring Jewish Center case are ongoing.
entries.author: Kendall Staton

entries.title: Trump And Republicans Start Racing To Confirm Judges
entries.summary: Democrats objected to the speed of nominations for a DOJ official and a defeated Texas Supreme Court candidate.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump and Senate Republicans started a rush Tuesday to confirm as many judicial nominees as possible before they lose their majority in January, including the announcement of three new nominees.

The Senate Judiciary Committee voted to advance four judicial nominees to the Senate floor, teed up more committee votes on six other pending bench picks and held a confirmation hearing for another four.

Trump then announced new nominees for the Texas and South Carolina federal bench in three Truth Social posts. Word had already gotten out about two of the nominees because they had submitted confirmation paperwork to the committee just after Democrats won control of the Senate in the midterms.

That includes James Sullivan, who lost his race to be reelected to the Texas Supreme Court. “Senators Ted Cruz and John Cornyn highly recommend him!” Trump said of Sullivan.

Cornyn posted on X after Tuesday’s meeting to reiterate his support for Sullivan: “An election result does not diminish a record of ability and integrity. He should be confirmed.”

That support was not noted for Elliot Gaiser, head of the Department of Justice’s Office of Legal Counsel, who Cornyn had reportedly said did not go through the “usual process” of judicial selection in the state.

Gaiser wrote in the paperwork that he was contacted by Cruz’s staff the day after the election, discussed a possible nomination with Cornyn’s staff on Nov. 6 and was contacted by the White House that same day.

Sen. Dick Durbin of Illinois, the top Democrat on the panel, said Republicans were breaking the rules by trying to jam judicial nominees into positions of the federal district court before Sen.-elect James Talarico (D-Texas) is sworn in on Jan. 3 and would have sway over who is selected.

"The defeat of the Republicans in Texas has created a scramble for lifetime appointments to the federal bench," Durbin said.

Committee Chair Chuck Grassley said during Tuesday’s committee action that he intends to move as quickly as possible — and there is no committee rule against moving fast on confirmations.

Grassley also accused Democrats of using “unprecedented levels of obstruction to stall” the process of confirming the president’s nominees.

“Considering judicial nominations is some of the most important work that this committee does,” Grassley said. “As chairman, it’s been my priority to ensure that the federal benches are filled with judges who will uphold our constitutional rule of law.”

Trump also indicated in a social media post that judges should be a priority for Republicans: “Very important for the U.S. Senate to confirm all of our pending 161 Nominations, including 25 Federal Judges.”

Cornyn told The Washington Sun he’s unsure if Republicans will be able to push all of the president’s remaining nominees through to confirmation in time.

“That’s going to be very hard,” Cornyn said. “But I think we ought to get as many people as we can.”

Sen. Cory Booker (D-New Jersey) told The Sun that he’s “frustrated” with Trump’s recent nominees for judgeships and warned his Republican colleagues against breaking Senate norms to speed through the empty bench seats.

“The people of Texas have spoken,” Booker said. “Now we’re seeing Texas leadership, through Trump … trying to take advantage of the process and shove through a lot of judges to keep James Talarico from having a say.”

And Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Connecticut) said some of Trump’s recent nominations are attempts to place politically “compromised” judges on the federal bench, such as former administration officials.

“They’re nominated because of their political positions and their personal loyalties, and perhaps their involvement in corrupt schemes,” Blumenthal said. “Because the Department of Justice has become an enabler for corruption in this administration.”
entries.author: Ellie Fivas
